title: Your Soft Skills Baseline — College & Early Career
theme: Real decisions from Indian campuses, internships, and first jobs
description: An 8-round baseline assessment designed for college students and early career professionals. Scenarios reflect real challenges in Indian campuses, internships, and first jobs. No right or wrong answers — just honest choices. Takes about 10 minutes.
target_audience: College students and early career professionals aged 18-25
learning_objectives: Understand your natural response style across 8 key soft skill dimensions
See how you handle workplace pressure, ethical dilemmas, and career decisions
Identify where you're already strong and where you can grow
how_to_play: Read each situation carefully and pick the response that feels most like what you would actually do — not what you think the ideal answer is. Honest choices give you the most useful result.
psychological_framework: Situational judgment assessment based on behavioral decision theory

glossary_terms.definition: The process of choosing between different options after considering their consequences
Giving up one thing to gain another — every choice has a cost
A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term goal
The result or outcome of a choice or action
A particular way of looking at something — everyone has a different perspective

rounds.title: The Internship Mistake
rounds.story: You're 3 weeks into your first internship at a Bengaluru fintech startup. In a rush to meet a deadline, you forwarded a data analysis report to the leadership team — but you later realize it contained a critical calculation error that overstated revenue by 40%. The CEO has already referenced your numbers in a board meeting. Your manager Priya hasn't noticed yet.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the error before it causes bigger damage
rounds.coaching_moment: How you respond when you've made a high-stakes mistake at work reveals more about your character than almost any other professional situation — especially early in your career.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever made a mistake at work or college that you were tempted to hide? What did you end up doing, and how did it feel?

choices.label: Go directly to Priya, acknowledge the error, and bring a corrected version of the report
choices.feedback: Coming forward immediately takes real courage when you're three weeks in and still proving yourself. But this is the only path that protects the company from compounding the error further and protects you from a much worse outcome later. Most managers — even when frustrated — respect the intern who caught and owned their own mistake.
choices.coaching_moment: Owning a mistake early, before it compounds, is not weakness — it is the foundational professional act that separates people who grow quickly from those who don't. The cost of transparency is almost always lower than the cost of concealment.

choices.label: Quietly fix the numbers in your own copy and say nothing unless someone brings it up
choices.feedback: Fixing it silently might feel like damage control, but if the error has already been cited in a board meeting, the incorrect numbers exist in places you can't retroactively fix. If someone later traces the source back to you — and in a fintech startup, they will — the cover-up becomes far worse than the original mistake.
choices.coaching_moment: Silence after a consequential error is only ever a delay, not a resolution. The longer the gap between the mistake and the correction, the harder the conversation becomes.

choices.label: Wait and monitor — if no one asks, the board discussion may not lead to anything serious
choices.feedback: Waiting to see if anyone notices is the highest-risk choice of the three, even though it feels like the safest in the moment. A 40% revenue overstatement in a Series A fintech could trigger decisions — hiring, fundraising, procurement — based on false data. The later this surfaces, the more serious the professional and legal consequences.
choices.coaching_moment: Hoping a problem goes away without action is not patience — it is avoidance. The professional who acts on a hard truth early is always in a better position than one who waits for someone else to find it.

rounds.image_prompt: young professional at laptop in a startup open office in Bengaluru, looking stressed at a spreadsheet with a visible error highlighted in red
rounds.scene_hint: Bengaluru startup, open office, urgent moment, first internship pressure

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Free-Rider Problem
rounds.story: It's final semester and your 4-person project group has an important presentation worth 30% of your grade. Two members — including your close friend Rohan — have contributed almost nothing for three months but now demand equal credit on the submission. Your professor has no visibility into individual contributions, and the deadline is in two days.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle credit and contribution before submission
rounds.coaching_moment: How you respond when fairness and friendship conflict is one of the earliest tests of your professional values — and the pattern you establish here tends to follow you into your career.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever let a free-rider situation slide to preserve a friendship or avoid conflict? What was the long-term impact on the relationship?

choices.label: Document everyone's actual contributions carefully and approach the professor privately before submission
choices.feedback: Going to the professor with documented evidence is the most strategically sound and ethically consistent choice. It protects the grade of people who actually worked and creates an accurate record. The discomfort of this conversation is real — but allowing unequal work to receive equal credit normalises free-riding and damages the group's trust in each other.
choices.coaching_moment: Documenting contributions and communicating through proper channels is not 'telling on' someone — it is ensuring that outcomes reflect reality. That's a professional skill, not a social betrayal.

choices.label: Let it go and give everyone equal credit — the friendship means more than the marks difference
choices.feedback: The instinct to preserve the relationship is understandable, but letting free-riders receive full credit without any conversation doesn't preserve the friendship — it creates a quiet resentment that typically surfaces later. And for Rohan, it removes any feedback that would have helped him show up differently next time.
choices.coaching_moment: Avoiding conflict is not the same as resolving it. When you absorb someone's unfair behaviour without acknowledgment, you are training them to repeat it — and training yourself to accept it.

choices.label: Confront the issue directly in the group's next meeting — everyone should hear this conversation together
choices.feedback: A group conversation creates shared accountability, which is valuable. The risk is that a public confrontation — especially when your close friend is involved — can quickly become defensive and produce more heat than resolution. With two days left, a private conversation with Rohan before the group meeting might make that meeting far more productive.
choices.coaching_moment: Group conversations about contribution work well when the groundwork has been laid privately first. A public confrontation without preparation often hardens positions instead of shifting them.

rounds.scene_hint: college campus, group project tension, final semester deadline pressure

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Startup vs. Placement
rounds.story: You have 6 months left in college. A senior alumnus from IIT Bombay wants you to join his early-stage startup as a founding team member — equity stake plus a below-market salary of ₹3.5 LPA. Placement season is starting and TCS, Infosys, and Wipro are offering ₹6-7 LPA packages with stability. Your parents took education loans and are counting on you to help repay them quickly.
rounds.goal: Decide which path to take at this career crossroads
rounds.coaching_moment: Very few decisions in your early career will be purely about the money or purely about the opportunity — most of the meaningful ones sit at the intersection of both, and force you to understand what you actually value.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you picture your career five years from now, what matters more to you — security and steady progress, or upside potential and a higher chance of something extraordinary?

choices.label: Join the startup — the equity and founding experience are worth the financial risk
choices.feedback: This is a high-conviction, high-risk bet on yourself and the founding team. Founding-stage experience is genuinely rare and difficult to replicate — but so is the financial pressure of telling your parents the loan repayment will take longer. This choice is only right if you've genuinely evaluated the team, the product, and your own ability to absorb the financial constraint.
choices.coaching_moment: Taking a calculated risk early in your career — when your financial obligations are still manageable — is often a better window than you think. The key word is 'calculated': base the decision on what you know about the team, not just the narrative.

choices.label: Take the campus placement — a stable foundation first, startup opportunities will come later
choices.feedback: Choosing stability given your family's financial situation is entirely rational and not a failure of ambition. Many successful founders did corporate stints first. The one thing to watch: 'stability first' is only a stepping stone if you actually use the stable period to build skills and stay connected to your entrepreneurial instincts — rather than letting inertia take over.
choices.coaching_moment: Taking a safe first job with intention is a completely valid strategy. The risk is not the choice itself — it is letting the comfort of the stable job become a reason to stop asking the bigger questions.

choices.label: Participate in placements and keep the startup conversation open — see both options through before deciding
choices.feedback: Running both tracks in parallel keeps your options alive and gives you real information before committing. It also signals to the startup founder that you are serious enough to do due diligence rather than leap impulsively — most good founders respect that. The main risk is doing neither track well; keeping your options open only works if you are genuinely committed to both processes.
choices.coaching_moment: Gathering real data before a life-stage decision is not indecision — it is good judgment. Just make sure 'keeping options open' is active exploration, not a way to avoid committing to anything.

rounds.image_prompt: young Indian professional looking at two paths — a corporate campus and a startup office — with a thoughtful expression
rounds.scene_hint: campus placement fair, career crossroads, family pressure and ambition in tension

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: The Borrowed Idea
rounds.story: Your internship manager Vikram suggests that to secure a Pre-Placement Offer, you should present a product improvement idea to the head of product next week. The catch: the idea was originally pitched by a junior intern named Aisha two weeks ago in a team brainstorm — Vikram says 'everyone does this' and that Aisha won't mind since she's leaving after her internship anyway. The presentation is in two days.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the credit question before the presentation
rounds.coaching_moment: How you handle attribution early in your career — especially when a senior person is telling you it doesn't matter — defines the professional reputation you will spend the next decade building.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever received credit for something that wasn't entirely yours, or seen someone else take credit for your work? How did each of those feel?

choices.label: Present the idea and explicitly attribute it to Aisha — use the presentation to show how you've developed it further
choices.feedback: Attributing the original idea to Aisha while demonstrating your own analytical contribution is not just the ethical path — it's the strategically strongest one. Product heads notice people who handle credit generously. It signals confidence, integrity, and the kind of collaborative instinct that companies actually promote into leadership.
choices.coaching_moment: Giving credit where it's due and still showing your own contribution is not a trade-off — it is the clearest signal that you are someone safe to give responsibility to. Integrity in attribution is one of the most powerful career signals that exists.

choices.label: Decline to present — if you can't present it honestly, you won't present it at all
choices.feedback: Declining on principle is a strong ethical stand and reflects high personal standards. The trade-off is a missed PPO opportunity and potentially a strained relationship with Vikram. Before deciding, it is worth asking whether there is a version of this presentation — with proper attribution — that Vikram would accept. A flat refusal might close the door on an option that didn't need to be closed.
choices.coaching_moment: There is a difference between refusing to participate in something unethical and refusing to engage with the situation at all. The former is integrity; the latter is sometimes just avoidance dressed up as a principle.

choices.label: Present it as your own — it's a PPO opportunity and Aisha is leaving anyway
choices.feedback: This might work in the short term, but professional networks in Indian tech are much smaller than they appear. Aisha's leaving doesn't mean she's gone — she likely stays connected through alumni groups, LinkedIn, and mutual contacts. And beyond the risk: a career built on a habit of taking credit you haven't earned eventually collapses when people stop trusting you with their ideas.
choices.coaching_moment: Taking someone's idea without attribution might feel costless when they are no longer in the room. But your reputation is built on what you do consistently, not just what you get away with once.

rounds.scene_hint: startup office, internship PPO pressure, credit and attribution dilemma

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Friend Group Drift
rounds.story: Your close college friend group has started spending heavily — weekend trips to Goa, expensive restaurants in Koramangala, the latest iPhones. You're on a tight stipend of ₹8,000 a month from your internship and are actively trying to save. They've started excluding you from plans, and a few subtle comments have crept in about you being 'boring' or 'too cautious.' You value these friendships deeply.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the growing gap in financial circumstances
rounds.coaching_moment: The ability to hold your ground on financial decisions while maintaining the relationships that matter to you is a form of resilience that very few people develop before they are forced to.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Has there been a time when social pressure caused you to spend money you didn't have? What was the real cost — financial and emotional?

choices.label: Be honest with the group about your budget and suggest alternatives that work for everyone
choices.feedback: Naming your situation clearly — without apology, but without dramatising it — is both the most honest and the most practically useful move. Friends who respond by excluding you or mocking you after you've been direct about your constraints are telling you something important about the friendship. Friends who adjust are worth keeping.
choices.coaching_moment: Saying 'I'm on a budget this month — let's find something that works for everyone' is not an embarrassing confession. It is a socially mature act that most people in their twenties are too anxious to make. The ones who do it tend to attract better friendships.

choices.label: Spend anyway — FOMO is real and you don't want to lose these friendships over money
choices.feedback: The fear of losing friendships is real and the social cost of opting out repeatedly is not nothing. But spending money you don't have to maintain friendships that require it is a pattern that compounds quickly. Stipend-to-EMI spirals typically start here — and the financial stress it creates usually damages the friendships far more than honest budget conversations ever would.
choices.coaching_moment: Spending to belong is a substitute for the harder and more valuable act of communicating honestly. Friendships strong enough to survive 'I can't afford this right now' are the ones worth protecting.

choices.label: Start withdrawing quietly and invest the time and energy in building new connections
choices.feedback: Moving on from a friend group that no longer fits your circumstances is sometimes the right call — but doing it silently, without a conversation, tends to create lingering bitterness on both sides. Before you start drifting, it is worth asking whether one honest conversation might have changed the dynamic.
choices.coaching_moment: Quietly exiting a relationship to avoid a difficult conversation is a pattern that follows you from one group to the next. Before you leave, consider whether you have given the friendship the honest signal it needed to adapt.

rounds.image_prompt: young person looking at a restaurant group photo on Instagram with a tight expression, budget spreadsheet visible on desk
rounds.scene_hint: Bengaluru, stipend life, social pressure vs financial discipline

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Salary Conversation
rounds.story: After three interview rounds, you've received an offer from a mid-size Pune company. The CTC is ₹4.8 LPA — about 20% below what your market research shows for this role. The HR, Meenakshi, says 'this is our standard for freshers' but hints there is 'some flexibility.' You genuinely want this role and have no competing offers right now.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond to the offer
rounds.coaching_moment: The first salary negotiation of your career sets a reference point that compounds over time — a 15% increase at ₹4.8 LPA creates a very different trajectory than the same percentage increase at ₹5.8 LPA, for decades.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever not asked for something you wanted professionally because you were afraid of being turned down or seeming greedy? What did you do instead?

choices.label: Counter confidently with a specific number backed by market data — 'Based on benchmarks, I was targeting ₹5.8 LPA'
choices.feedback: A specific, researched counter — offered calmly and without ultimatum — is almost always received better than candidates expect. HR professionals anticipate negotiation for entry-level roles; a well-prepared ask does not put offers at risk, it signals that you understand your own market value. The worst realistic outcome is 'this is our firm cap' — and then you have full information to decide.
choices.coaching_moment: Most first-time negotiators never try because they fear losing the offer — but the actual risk of a polite, data-backed counter for a graduate role is very close to zero. What you lose by not asking is real; what you risk by asking is usually imagined.

choices.label: Accept immediately — you don't want to risk losing the offer by seeming difficult
choices.feedback: Accepting quickly to avoid risk is understandable, especially when you have no other offers. But the framing matters: accepting without negotiating is not playing it safe — it is paying a fixed cost (a lower starting salary) to avoid an imagined risk (an offer withdrawal that almost never actually happens for polite counters). That trade-off rarely favours acceptance.
choices.coaching_moment: Mistaking discomfort for danger is one of the most common ways people cost themselves money early in their careers. The feeling of risk in a salary negotiation is almost always bigger than the actual risk.

choices.label: Ask about non-monetary benefits — flexible work, learning allowance, or faster review cycles
choices.feedback: This is a creative and often underused approach. Non-salary benefits can have significant financial and developmental value — a ₹30,000 learning stipend, an extra day of remote work per week, or a 6-month instead of 12-month review cycle can compound meaningfully. And HR teams often have more flexibility on these than on base salary. It is a strong move if you are genuinely interested in those things.
choices.coaching_moment: Total compensation is broader than CTC. Asking for non-monetary value — especially things that accelerate your growth — can be more valuable than a base salary bump in the first year, and it signals that you think long-term about your own development.

rounds.image_prompt: young professional on a video call with HR, offer letter visible on screen, preparing to respond thoughtfully
rounds.scene_hint: Pune job offer, first salary negotiation, nervousness and opportunity

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Long-Distance Choice
rounds.story: You've been selected for a 6-month fully-funded fellowship in Singapore — competitive, resume-defining, and career-transforming. Your partner Aryan of two years is in the middle of a difficult career transition and is strongly against you going. He says he needs your support and is unsure whether the relationship can survive long distance. You have 10 days to accept.
rounds.goal: Decide how to move forward when career and relationship point in opposite directions
rounds.coaching_moment: There is no objectively correct answer here — but how you make the decision reveals whether you think through your own priorities clearly, or let urgency and guilt do your thinking for you.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever made a major life decision to avoid disappointing someone else? How did it turn out — for the relationship, and for you?

choices.label: Accept the fellowship — your career growth is a legitimate priority and this window won't come back
choices.feedback: Prioritising a rare career opportunity is a legitimate and defensible choice. Relationships that cannot survive one partner growing are worth examining honestly. The key question is whether this is a decision you are making from clarity and conviction, or one you are making because the fellowship is easier than the relationship conversation — those are very different.
choices.coaching_moment: Choosing your own growth is not selfish — it is necessary. A partner who requires you to decline once-in-a-decade opportunities as the price of the relationship is asking something that will cost you more over time than a six-month separation.

choices.label: Decline — Aryan needs you right now and the relationship matters more than the fellowship
choices.feedback: Choosing to stay for someone you love during a genuinely difficult period is a meaningful act of care. The question to sit with honestly is whether declining is a genuine choice you can make without resentment — or whether it is a choice you are making from anxiety about Aryan's reaction. Decisions made from fear of the other person's response are not really free choices, and they tend to generate long-term resentment.
choices.coaching_moment: Staying for someone is only a gift if it is freely given. If there is a part of you that will track this sacrifice and hold it against the relationship later, it is worth having that honest conversation with yourself before you decline.

choices.label: Explore whether a remote-first or deferred option exists before making a final decision
choices.feedback: Before accepting a binary choice, it is worth checking whether the binary is real. Many fellowships have more flexibility than their initial terms suggest — especially for exceptional candidates. Asking about a deferred start, a remote component for part of the period, or a phased arrangement costs nothing and sometimes changes the decision entirely.
choices.coaching_moment: Most people treat the options presented to them as the full set of options. Before accepting a dilemma, it is always worth asking whether the structure of the choice itself can be changed.

rounds.scene_hint: career vs relationship dilemma, Singapore fellowship, ten-day deadline

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Metrics Lie
rounds.story: Two weeks before your startup's Series A pitch, you discover that the engagement metrics the team has been sharing with investors are artificially inflated — your co-founder Siddharth has been counting bot traffic as active users. You are not involved in the decision and did not create the numbers. The round could raise ₹5 crore that would secure jobs for 15 employees, including yours.
rounds.goal: Decide what to do with this information before the funding round closes
rounds.coaching_moment: The hardest ethical tests are the ones where doing the right thing has a direct and immediate cost to people you care about — including yourself. That is exactly when values are revealed.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever known about something dishonest happening at an organisation you were part of? What did you do, and what did the decision cost you?

choices.label: Raise it directly with Siddharth first — give him the chance to correct the numbers before the pitch
choices.feedback: Going to Siddharth first is both the ethically proportionate and the strategically sensible first move. It gives him the chance to correct the record before investors are misled, and it keeps the problem within the team. If he refuses or dismisses the concern, you have clearer information about your own situation — and clearer moral standing to escalate. This sequence matters.
choices.coaching_moment: Confronting someone directly and privately before escalating is almost always the right sequence — not because it protects them, but because it respects the principle that people deserve the chance to correct their own mistakes before others intervene.

choices.label: Report the discrepancy anonymously to the lead investor before the pitch closes
choices.feedback: Alerting investors directly prevents them from making a decision on false data — and that is a real moral obligation. The risk is that anonymous reporting without first giving Siddharth the chance to respond bypasses an important step. If it later emerges that you knew and went external without talking to him first, it will raise questions about your own judgment and loyalty, even if your intent was honest.
choices.coaching_moment: External disclosure is sometimes the right move — but in most cases it is strongest when you have already tried the internal conversation first. Skipping that step is not just a procedural issue; it changes how the disclosure is received and remembered.

choices.label: Stay silent — too much is at stake for 15 employees and you are not the one who made the decision
choices.feedback: The scale of what is at stake is real, and so is the argument that you did not create the problem. But staying silent makes you complicit in investor fraud — not legally responsible in the same way as Siddharth, but knowingly part of a deceptive transaction. If the round closes on false metrics and the fraud is later discovered, 'I knew but said nothing' is a very difficult position to defend professionally or personally.
choices.coaching_moment: Inaction in the face of harm is still a choice — and it is one with consequences. 'I didn't create the problem' is true, but 'I knew and chose not to act' is also true. Both things can be true at the same time, and both matter.

achievements.title: Baseline Established
achievements.description: Completed your College & Early Career Soft Skills Baseline

transfer_exercises: This week, notice one moment where you stayed silent about something that felt wrong — at work, in a team, or in a conversation. Write down what stopped you from speaking up and what it would have cost you to say something.
Think of one person in your professional life whose work or ideas you have benefited from without explicitly acknowledging it. Find a small, genuine way to give them credit this week.
Next time you face a financial or career decision under social pressure, pause for 24 hours before responding. Write down what you actually want before you check what other people expect.
target_age: College students and early career professionals aged 18-25
coaching_moment: Every choice shapes your strategy — great leaders think several steps ahead before deciding.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
